about: How words that are not flags bind to declared arguments. Arguments fill in declaration order; a variadic takes everything left over.

vectors.doc: A required argument takes the first non-flag word.
A required argument with nothing to fill it is an error.
An optional argument left unfilled is simply absent.
Two arguments fill in declaration order, regardless of what the values look like.
Flags and positionals may interleave; a flag between two words does not change which argument each word fills.
More words than there are arguments to hold them is an error, not silent truncation.
A variadic argument collects every remaining word.
A fixed argument is filled before a following variadic starts collecting.
An optional variadic given nothing is absent rather than an empty list.
`var_min` is enforced: too few values is an error.
`var_max` is enforced: too many values is an error.

reference.diverges: usage-lib reports `unexpected_arg`. The outcome is the same rejection; the distinct code is what tells a caller the limit was a `var_max` rather than an absent argument.

vectors.doc: A negative number is a value, not an unknown flag. A leading `-` followed by a digit cannot begin a flag name, so the token is offered to the next argument.

`var_max` is a limit on how many words a variadic takes, not only a check on how many it got: once it is full the next argument gets the rest. Without that, `[a]… [b]` could never be filled, and clap's `num_args` — which every generated spec comes from — behaves this way.
vectors.spec:
name "ex"
bin "ex"
arg "[a]" var=#true var_max=1
arg "[b]"

vectors.doc: The bound stops the variadic even when nothing follows it, so the extra word has nowhere to go and is an error rather than a silently dropped value.
Unbounded is the common case and unchanged: nothing after it can be filled, which is why declaring an argument there is refused.
The same rule for a flag whose one occurrence collects: `--include` takes the two words its bound allows, and the third is the positional's.

reference.diverges: usage-lib does not collect for a variadic flag at all — it takes one value, so `b` fills [out] and `c` is unexpected. The same gap as `long-variadic-flag-arg`, which the spec reference documents; bounding what usage-argv collects is consistent with it collecting in the first place.
